newsitem.title: GERMANY: German North-Rhine metal sector agrees pay deal.
newsitem.headline: German North-Rhine metal sector agrees pay deal.

text.p: The IG Metall trade union and employers in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, the largest region in Germany's metal and engineering industry, said on Wednesday they had reached a wage deal.

The two sides said they had agreed a package for the some 850,000 workers in the region which did not implement cuts to sick payments made possible by a new federal law, and which set wages for the next two years.
Under the package, wages will rise 1.5 percent from April 1 1997 and a further 2.5 percent the year after. A 200 mark lump sum payment will be made for the first three months of 1997.

The deal mirrors an accord signed in the state of Lower Saxony last Thursday, which employers estimated would result in a rise in labour-related costs of less than one percent in 1997, with a small further rise in 1998.

The earlier deal was widely seen as a breakthrough in the pay dispute that has affected the sector since employers said they would try to put into effect a new law cutting sick payments by 20 percent.
Unlike the Lower Saxony deal, the traditionally generous Christmas bonuses in the sector will fluctuate between 50 and 65 percent depending on the rate of absenteeism in a specific company.
Current Christmas bonuses stand at around 60 percent of a monthly salary, a payment that the Lower Saxony agreement cut to a standard 55 percent.
Union and employer officials said they had also agreed "wide-ranging" job protection measures in the industry, which nationwide has been losing jobs at a rate of around 100,000 a month.
